title: How We Know Ahom History
content: Buranjis in Tai-Ahom and Assamese: authorship, manuscript families, copying, translation, and court purposes.
Inscriptions, copper plates, coins, archaeology, diplomatic letters, religious literature, genealogies, and material culture.
Persian, Burmese, British, and other external accounts: what each can and cannot establish.
Colonial, nationalist, regional, community, and recent academic interpretations; missing voices and archival silences.
Rules for separating documented events, probable reconstructions, oral traditions, legends, and modern commemorative claims.
visual: Source-family diagram and a sample comparison of conflicting accounts.

title: The Brahmaputra Valley on the Eve of 1228
content: River systems, floodplains, forests, hill passages, wet-rice zones, and travel constraints.
Political landscape after the fragmentation of Kamarupa; distinguish later state boundaries from medieval ones.
Moran, Borahi, Chutiya, Kachari/Dimasa, Bhuyan, and other communities: their own histories and changing relationships.
Existing settlement, cultivation, exchange, religion, and languages before Ahom arrival.
How geography shaped the possibilities for state formation, warfare, and diplomacy.
visual: A background map with approximate political zones and a river-and-route map.

title: Tai Origins and Royal Ancestry
content: Tai-speaking worlds, Mong Mao and related regional polities, migration traditions, and historical geography.
Sukaphaa’s ancestry, titles, companions, and variant genealogies; document what is uncertain.
Khunlung–Khunlai and divine-origin narratives as traditions of legitimacy rather than dated political fact.
Language, ritual specialists, agricultural knowledge, and forms of leadership carried into Assam.
Relationship between Tai-Ahom identity, the royal dynasty, and the later multi-community kingdom.
visual: An annotated genealogy and a map of the proposed homeland and routes.

title: Across the Patkai: Arrival in 1228
content: Competing accounts of departure, migration stages, route, companions, animals, and dates.
Patkai crossings and encounters with frontier communities, including both negotiation and violence where supported.
Arrival in the Brahmaputra valley and the conventional significance of 1228.
Settlement choices, river crossings, scouting, food supply, and adaptation.
Identify later heroic additions and unsupported numerical claims in popular accounts.
visual: A route map marking secure, approximate, and disputed locations separately.

title: Sukaphaa and the Founding Kingdom
content: Settlement phases, the establishment of Charaideo, and the growth of the first court.
Moran and Borahi relations: alliances, intermarriage, conflict, incorporation, and local agency.
Early institutions, leading officers, land, rice cultivation, labour, and royal household.
The foundations of kingship, ritual life, succession, and historical record keeping.
Sukaphaa’s death, succession, funerary traditions, and the difference between contemporary evidence and later memory.
visual: A settlement sequence and early-state institutional diagram.

title: The First Successors: Suteuphaa, Subinphaa, and Sukhaangphaa
content: Individual reign dossiers for Suteuphaa, Subinphaa, and Sukhaangphaa, including alternate spellings.
Early territorial consolidation and relations with neighbouring rulers and communities.
Royal lineages, clan traditions, nobles, and succession arrangements.
Cultivation, population incorporation, and development of settlements and offices.
Short notices and uncertain episodes retained in an appendix rather than inflated into invented narratives.
visual: A succession chart and comparative reign table.

title: Succession Crises and Rule without a King
content: Sukhrangphaa, Sutuphaa, and Tyao Khamti: separate biographies and reign narratives.
Political roles of nobles, royal households, and competing claimants.
Interregna: who exercised authority, why a ruler was not installed, and what sources say.
Assassination traditions, external encounters, and chronology disagreements.
Institutional continuity despite disputed succession; avoid assuming the state ceased to exist during an interregnum.
visual: A king-and-interregnum timeline with competing date columns.

title: Sudangphaa: The Bamuni Konwar
content: Childhood and upbringing traditions, recovery of royal identity, and accession.
Brahmanical influence, court ritual, royal legitimacy, and limits of claims about an abrupt religious conversion.
Noble opposition and the political consolidation of the reign.
Frontier diplomacy, campaigns, and agreements attributed to this ruler.
Death, succession, and the later significance of the Bamuni Konwar story.
visual: An accession narrative with evidence labels and a frontier map.

title: The Fifteenth-Century Kingdom
content: Individual sections for Sujangphaa, Suphakphaa, Susenphaa, Suhenphaa, and Supimphaa.
Frontier relations, campaigns, internal conflict, and succession changes under each ruler.
Settlement, cultivation, administrative growth, and integration of communities.
Noble families, royal kinship, court violence, and competing historical explanations.
A complete catalogue of smaller recorded events and gaps in surviving documentation.
visual: Five ruler dossiers and a map showing changes in the eastern kingdom.

title: Suhungmung and a Larger State
content: Accession, royal names and titles, household, court, and political ambitions.
Territorial growth as a series of campaigns and negotiations, not one uniform conquest.
Administrative innovations, regional offices, settlement, and incorporation of new populations.
Changes in royal language, titles, religious patronage, and political identity.
Opposition, succession struggle, death, and an assessment of the reign through multiple source traditions.
visual: A before-and-after territorial map with dated layers.

title: The Chutiya Kingdom and Ahom Expansion
content: Chutiya political history and institutions before incorporation; include Chutiya perspectives.
Campaign sequence, rulers, commanders, locations, and disputed dates.
Traditions concerning Sati Sadhani/Sadhini: distinguish documentary history, oral tradition, and commemoration.
Sadiya administration, population movements, craft knowledge, religious sites, and military resources.
Resistance, accommodation, and long-term changes after conquest.
visual: A campaign map and a comparison of Ahom and Chutiya narratives.

title: Ahom–Kachari/Dimasa Relations
content: Kachari/Dimasa political geography and the significance of Dimapur and later centres.
Campaigns, commanders, diplomatic demands, settlements, and relocations.
Weapons, forts, river routes, and limits of battlefield reconstructions.
Consequences for trade, frontier control, population, and administration.
Distinguish the histories of neighbouring peoples from a narrative told only from the Ahom court.
visual: A changing-frontier map and campaign-and-treaty table.

title: Bengal Campaigns, Turbak, and Mula Gabharu
content: Bengal’s political context and the sequence of invasions and counter-campaigns.
Turbak, Ahom commanders, military adaptations, and the battles recorded in different accounts.
Mula Gabharu’s life, actions, source history, and later representation.
Captives, settlement, craft skills, religious communities, and the aftermath of warfare.
Check famous speeches, casualty totals, battle locations, and claims about the origins of institutions.
visual: A campaign atlas page and a Mula Gabharu evidence dossier.

title: Suklenmung and Garhgaon
content: Accession, lineage, major officers, and the structure of the court.
The development of Garhgaon: landscape, defence, settlement, and royal space.
Campaigns, frontier consolidation, roads, and other works attributed to the reign.
Coins, inscriptions, titles, and religious patronage where surviving evidence permits.
Death, succession, and links between the expanded state and its next phase.
visual: A capital map and catalogue of securely attributed material evidence.

title: Sukhaamphaa and the Koch Challenge
content: The long reign and the Khora Raja tradition; royal kinship and principal officers.
Nara Narayan, Chilarai, Koch power, and the sequence of Ahom–Koch confrontations.
Defeat, terms of settlement, hostages, tribute, and political recovery.
Territorial limits, frontier security, alliances, and the later division of Koch power.
Long-term consequences for relations with Bengal and the emerging Mughal frontier.
visual: An Ahom–Koch comparison and a dated frontier sequence.

title: Diplomacy and the Regional Order before 1603
content: Comparative relations with Kamata/Koch, Chutiya, Kachari/Dimasa, Bhuyans, and eastern Tai polities.
Envoys, marriage, gifts, tribute, hostage arrangements, written agreements, and ceremonial ranking.
Markets, passes, buffer zones, and the difference between tribute and direct administration.
Periodic conflict and negotiation with hill and frontier communities; terminology must be historically explained.
A source-backed register of every recoverable diplomatic mission before 1603.
visual: A diplomatic-network map and mission register.
